p.src: Now, while Concubine Zhao was speaking with Jia Zheng, they suddenly heard a crash outside, though they could not tell what had caused it. When they hurriedly asked what had happened, they learned that the outer window frame had not been properly fastened; it had collapsed, wrenching its hinges loose and hanging down. Concubine Zhao scolded the maids, then went with them to set it right before returning to see Jia Zheng settled for the night. There is no need to dwell on this.

p.src: Meanwhile, in Happy Red Court, Baoyu had only just gone to bed, and the maids were about to disperse for the night when they suddenly heard someone knocking at the courtyard gate. An old serving woman opened the gate and saw that it was Xia Que, a maid from Concubine Zhao's quarters. Asked what she wanted, Xia Que gave no answer but went straight inside to find Baoyu. Baoyu had only just lain down, and Qingwen and the others were still sitting beside his bed, laughing and joking. When they saw Xia Que, they all asked, “What is it? What brings you running here at this hour?” Smiling, Xia Que said to Baoyu, “I've come to give you a warning. Just now, our mistress said such-and-such about you in front of Master. Be on your guard when Master questions you tomorrow.” With that, she turned and left. Xiren called after her to stay for some tea, but Xia Que was afraid the gates would be shut, so she went straight home.

p.src: On hearing this, Baoyu felt like the Great Sage Sun when the tightening spell was recited: at once, neither his limbs nor his innermost organs felt at ease. He thought it over and over, but there was nothing else he could do; he had better master his books and prepare for tomorrow's examination. If he could recite without stumbling, then even if there were other charges against him, he might be able to fend off half of them. Having reached this conclusion, he hurriedly threw on his clothes, got up, and prepared to study. At the same time, he bitterly regretted that, thinking the matter had been dropped these past few days, he had let his lessons grow rusty again. Had he known, he would at least have reviewed a little every day. Taking stock of what he could still recite, he found that only the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean, and the two Analects were within his power to repeat together with their commentaries. Of the first book of Mencius, half was only imperfectly familiar; if someone suddenly quoted a line, he certainly could not continue it. As for the second book, he had forgotten well over half. As for the Five Classics, he had lately been composing poetry and therefore often read the Book of Songs. Though his understanding of it was not especially deep, it would still serve well enough to satisfy an inquiry. He remembered little of the others, but fortunately Jia Zheng had never ordered him to study them in the first place, so it would not matter greatly even if he knew nothing of them. Then there was classical prose: the pieces he had studied years ago—from the Zuo Commentary, the Strategies of the Warring States, the Gongyang and Guliang Commentaries, and writings of the Han and Tang—amounted to only a few dozen. Yet in recent years he had not reviewed so much as half a piece or a single phrase. Though he had occasionally browsed through them in idle moments, it had been no more than a passing whim; he forgot each thing as soon as he read it, and, having never applied himself, how could he possibly remember? There was no possible way to bluff his way through that. Worst of all was the matter of the contemporary eight-legged essay. He had always detested the form: it had not been devised by the sages, so how could it elucidate the subtlest depths of their teaching? It was merely a ladder by which later generations angled for fame and official gain. Although Jia Zheng had selected a hundred or so such essays before his departure and ordered Baoyu to read them, Baoyu had only occasionally glanced at one when some section or transition struck him as elegant, free-flowing, playful, or melancholy—something capable of stirring his feelings. Such reading merely entertained him for the moment; when had he ever studied a whole essay with concentrated care? If he reviewed this piece now, he feared he would be questioned on another tomorrow; if he reviewed that one, he feared he would be cross-examined on this. Besides, a single night's effort could never suffice to review everything. All this made him increasingly anxious and irritable. His own studying might not have mattered much, but it kept every maid in his rooms from sleeping. Naturally, the senior maids—Xiren, Sheyue, Qingwen, and the others—trimmed the candles and poured tea beside him, while the younger ones grew bleary-eyed with sleep and began nodding forward and backward. Qingwen scolded them: “You wretched little creatures! As if lying about like corpses day and night were never enough for you! The one time you have to stay up a little late, you start putting on this performance. If you keep this up, I'll give each of you a couple of jabs with a needle!”

p.src: Before she had finished speaking, there came a thud from the outer room. They hurried over to look and found that a young maid, dozing as she sat, had struck her head against the wall. Startled awake from her dream just as Qingwen uttered those words, the girl dazedly imagined that Qingwen had hit her and pleaded through her tears, “Dear sister, I promise I won't do it again.” Everyone burst out laughing. Baoyu quickly intervened: “Let her be. We really ought to send them all to bed. You should take turns getting some sleep too.” Xiren hurriedly said, “My precious young master, just attend to your own affairs. You have only this one night. For now, put your mind into these few books; once you are through this ordeal, you may occupy yourself with whatever else you please, and nothing will have been delayed.” Her earnest tone left Baoyu no choice but to resume his reading. He had read only a few lines when Sheyue poured another cup of tea to moisten his throat, and Baoyu took it and drank. Seeing that Sheyue wore only a short jacket and had removed her skirt, Baoyu said, “It is late and cold. You really ought to put on something warmer.” Smiling, Sheyue pointed at the book and said, “For the moment, forget all about us and give at least a little of your attention to that.”

p.src: Before she had finished speaking, Jinxing and Boli came running in through the rear door, crying, “Something terrible has happened! Someone just jumped down from the wall!” At this, everyone hurriedly asked where it had happened, called the servants up, and began searching everywhere. Qingwen had seen how miserable Baoyu was over his studies and how he had taxed his mind all night, though there was little hope of his being ready the next day. Just as she was trying to devise a way of extricating him from his predicament, this sudden alarm gave her an idea. She said to him, “Quick, take advantage of this and pretend to be ill. Say the fright has made you sick.” This was precisely what Baoyu wanted to hear. The night watchmen were therefore summoned, and they searched everywhere by lantern-light, but found no trace of anyone. They all said, “The young maids must have gone out half asleep and mistaken a branch swaying in the wind for a person.” Qingwen retorted, “Stop talking such damned nonsense! You did not search properly, and now, afraid you may be blamed, you are trying to fob us off with that excuse. It was not just one person who saw it. Baoyu and all of us had gone outside on an errand, and we witnessed it with our own eyes. Baoyu has now been so frightened that his face has changed color and his whole body is feverish. I must go to the main house at once to fetch him some pills to calm his spirit. When Madam asks about it, we shall have to give her a full account. Do you imagine the matter can simply be dropped because you say so?” The servants were too frightened to utter another word and had no choice but to search everywhere again. Qingwen and Boli duly went out to fetch the medicine, deliberately making such a commotion that everyone learned Baoyu had been frightened ill. When Lady Wang heard, she hurriedly sent someone to examine Baoyu and give him medicine. She also ordered the night watchmen to search carefully and had inquiries made among the pages who kept watch beyond the inner gate along the walls of the neighboring gardens. Thus lanterns and torches blazed throughout the Garden, and the uproar continued all night. At the fifth watch, the male and female stewards were summoned and ordered to investigate thoroughly and interrogate all the men and women who had been on watch inside and outside. When Grandmother Jia learned that Baoyu had been badly frightened, she questioned them closely about the cause. No one dared conceal the truth any longer, so they had to report the whole affair. Grandmother Jia said, “I knew something like this was bound to happen. That the night watchmen everywhere have grown careless is the least of it. For all we know, they may themselves be thieves.” Just then Lady Xing, Madam You, and the others came to pay their respects. Xifeng, Li Wan, and the young ladies were all in attendance. When they heard Grandmother Jia speak in this way, none of them made any reply. Tanchun alone stepped forward from her place and said with a smile, “Since Sister Xifeng has been unwell, the people in the Garden have grown far more unruly than before during these past few days. Formerly, they would merely steal a little time now and then; while sitting up on night duty, three or four of them might gather to throw dice or play cards. Such petty amusements were only meant to keep them awake. But lately they have become progressively more outrageous, actually setting up gambling dens with bankers and organizers, where the winnings and losses run to thirty, fifty, or even three hundred strings of cash. Only a fortnight ago, there was even a quarrel that ended in a fight.”

p.src: Grandmother Jia exclaimed, “If you knew about this, why did you not report it to us sooner?” Tanchun replied, “I thought Madam already had a great deal to attend to and had been unwell for several days, so I did not report it to her. I merely told Sister-in-law Li Wan and the household managers. They reprimanded the offenders several times, and things have improved somewhat lately.” Grandmother Jia said at once, “How could an unmarried girl like you understand the dangers involved? You take gambling to be a commonplace matter and suppose the only danger is that it may lead to quarrels. But you do not realize that once people gamble at night, there is no ensuring that they will not drink; and once they drink, doors and gates are inevitably unlocked whenever they please. They may go out to buy things or seek this person or that; in the stillness of the night, when few people are about, they can easily conceal thieves or entice adulterers and robbers inside. What wickedness might they not commit? Besides, the young ladies who live in the Garden are attended entirely by maids and married servants, good and bad all mixed together. Theft would be a small matter by comparison; if anything else should happen and one of the young ladies were even slightly implicated, the consequences would be grave. How can such a matter be treated leniently?” Hearing this, Tanchun silently returned to her seat. Xifeng had not yet fully recovered, and her illness had left her somewhat less energetic than usual. Now, hearing Grandmother Jia speak this way, she hastily said, “Just when this happens, I have to be ill!” She then turned and ordered someone to summon at once Lin Zhixiao’s wife and the other four women in charge of household affairs, whom she severely reprimanded in Grandmother Jia’s presence. Grandmother Jia ordered them to identify the gambling organizers and gamblers immediately. Anyone who informed on them would be rewarded, while anyone who concealed what they knew would be punished. Seeing that Grandmother Jia was angry, Lin Zhixiao’s wife and the others dared not show favoritism. They hurried to assemble everyone in the Garden and questioned them one by one. Although everyone tried denying it for a while, the truth inevitably came to light. They discovered three principal organizers, eight lesser ones, and more than twenty gamblers in all. All were brought before Grandmother Jia, where they knelt in the courtyard, knocking their heads loudly on the ground and begging for mercy. Grandmother Jia first asked the names of the principal organizers and how much money had been involved. It turned out that of these three principal organizers, one was related by marriage through her sister to Lin Zhixiao’s wife, another was the younger sister of Cook Liu’s wife in the Garden kitchen, and the third was Yingchun’s wet nurse. These three were the ringleaders; there were too many of the rest to record individually. Grandmother Jia ordered all the dice and cards to be burned. The confiscated money was to be distributed among the servants. Each ringleader was to receive forty strokes of the heavy bamboo, be expelled, and never be allowed to enter again. Each follower was to receive twenty strokes, forfeit three months’ wages, and be transferred to latrine duty. She also reprimanded Lin Zhixiao’s wife once more. Lin Zhixiao’s wife felt thoroughly embarrassed when she saw that her own relative had again brought shame upon her. Yingchun, who was present, also felt humiliated. Daiyu, Baochai, Tanchun, and the others, seeing Yingchun’s wet nurse in such a plight, felt sympathy for one of their own attendants. They all rose and smilingly pleaded with Grandmother Jia, “This nurse never ordinarily gambles. We do not know what came over her to make her join in on this one occasion.

p.src: Presently, when Grandmother Jia retired for her midday rest, everyone withdrew. Knowing that she was angry that day, however, none dared disperse and return home, so they had no choice but to wait there for the time being. Lady You went to Fengjie’s quarters and chatted with her for a while; but as Fengjie too was out of sorts, Lady You had to go into the garden to seek out the other ladies of the family for conversation. Lady Xing sat for a while with Lady Wang, then likewise went into the garden to take her mind off things. Just as she reached the garden gate, she saw a young maid from Grandmother Jia’s apartments, known as Silly Big Sister, coming along with a broad smile. She held a brightly colored object in her hand and, gazing down at it as she walked, failed to notice Lady Xing directly ahead. Only when she looked up and saw her did she stop. Lady Xing said, “You silly girl, what worthless trinket have you found to make you so happy? Bring it here and let me see.” This Silly Big Sister was in fact only fourteen or fifteen years old. She had recently been selected to serve on Grandmother Jia’s side, carrying water buckets, sweeping the courtyard, and doing other rough work. She was stout, with a broad face and two large feet, and performed heavy tasks briskly and efficiently. But she was also dull and obstinate, utterly ignorant, and her words and actions frequently overstepped the bounds of propriety. Grandmother Jia liked her brisk efficiency and also found her remarks amusing, so she named her “Simple Big Sister.” Whenever bored, she would summon the girl to provide a little laughter, speaking before her without the slightest reserve; hence the girl was also called “the Foolish Maid.” Even when she behaved discourteously, everyone saw how fond Grandmother Jia was of her and refrained from judging her too harshly. The maid benefited from this indulgence, and whenever Grandmother Jia did not summon her, she would go into the garden to play. That day, while digging for crickets in the garden, she happened to find behind a rockery a sachet embroidered in five colors. It was so splendid and finely wrought as to be most appealing, but what was embroidered on it was not flowers or birds: on one side were two stark-naked people entwined in an embrace, and on the other were several written characters. The foolish girl did not understand that it depicted an amorous scene and wondered to herself, “Could these be two demons fighting? If not, it must be a husband and wife quarrelling.” Unable to make sense of it however she tried, she was about to take it to show Grandmother Jia. Thus she walked along smiling and looking at it. When Lady Xing addressed her as she did, the girl laughed and said, “Your Ladyship has named it perfectly—it really is a thing even a dog wouldn’t recognize. Please take a look, Your Ladyship.” With that, she handed it over. Lady Xing took one look and, badly startled, immediately clenched it tight in her hand. “Where did you get this?” she demanded. Silly Big Sister replied, “I picked it up on the rockery while I was digging for crickets.” Lady Xing said, “Do not tell a single soul. This is a wicked thing, and you could be beaten to death for it too. You are spared only because everyone knows you have always been a simpleton. Never mention it again.” On hearing this, Silly Big Sister turned pale with fright and said, “I will never do it again.”

Grandmother Jia liked her brisk efficiency and also found her remarks amusing, so she named her “Simple Big Sister.” Whenever bored, she would summon the girl to provide a little laughter, speaking before her without the slightest reserve; hence the girl was also called “the Foolish Maid.”
Even when she behaved discourteously, everyone saw how fond Grandmother Jia was of her and refrained from judging her too harshly.
The maid benefited from this indulgence, and whenever Grandmother Jia did not summon her, she would go into the garden to play.

That day, while digging for crickets in the garden, she happened to find behind a rockery a sachet embroidered in five colors. It was so splendid and finely wrought as to be most appealing, but what was embroidered on it was not flowers or birds: on one side were two stark-naked people entwined in an embrace, and on the other were several written characters.
The foolish girl did not understand that it depicted an amorous scene and wondered to herself, “Could these be two demons fighting?
If not, it must be a husband and wife quarrelling.”

Unable to make sense of it however she tried, she was about to take it to show Grandmother Jia. Thus she walked along smiling and looking at it. When Lady Xing addressed her as she did, the girl laughed and said, “Your Ladyship has named it perfectly—it really is a thing even a dog wouldn’t recognize.
Please take a look, Your Ladyship.”
With that, she handed it over.
Lady Xing took one look and, badly startled, immediately clenched it tight in her hand. “Where did you get this?” she demanded.
Silly Big Sister replied, “I picked it up on the rockery while I was digging for crickets.”
Lady Xing said, “Do not tell a single soul.
This is a wicked thing, and you could be beaten to death for it too.
You are spared only because everyone knows you have always been a simpleton. Never mention it again.”
On hearing this, Silly Big Sister turned pale with fright and said, “I will never do it again.”

p.src: She kowtowed and went off in a daze. Lady Xing glanced back and saw that all those attending her were young girls, to whom she could not conveniently entrust the object. She therefore slipped it into her own sleeve. Deeply perplexed, she pondered where it could have come from, but betrayed nothing in her expression and proceeded to Yingchun’s rooms. Yingchun, already dispirited and troubled because her wet nurse had been found guilty, was suddenly informed that her mother had arrived and accordingly received her in the inner room. After tea had been served, Lady Xing said, “You are grown up now. When your nurse behaved in such a way, why did you not remonstrate with her? Everyone else has conducted themselves properly, yet one of our own people alone has done such a thing. What is the meaning of it?” Yingchun lowered her head and fingered the sash of her dress. After a long silence, she replied, “I spoke to her twice, but she would not listen, so there was nothing I could do. Besides, she is my nurse. It is for her to lecture me, not for me to lecture her.” “Nonsense!” said Lady Xing. If you behaved badly, it was naturally her duty to correct you. But now that she has broken the rules, you should have asserted your authority as her young mistress. If she dared disobey, you should have reported it to me. Why did you wait until outsiders knew all about it? Furthermore, since she was the one who ran the gambling pool, I fear she may have coaxed you into lending her hairpins, bracelets, clothes, or shoes to use as capital. You are so easily swayed and tenderhearted that you may well have helped her out with some things. If she has cheated you out of them, I have not a single coin to spare, so let us see how you will celebrate the festival tomorrow.” Yingchun said nothing and merely kept her head lowered as she fingered her sash. Seeing her like this, Lady Xing sneered, “It is all thanks to that admirable brother and sister-in-law of yours—that illustrious pair, Second Master Lian and Madam Feng! Husband and wife between them blot out heaven and cover the earth, and supposedly attend to everything, yet they pay no heed at all to their one and only sister. If you had come from my own body, there would be more to say—but as matters stand, I can only leave it to them. Besides, you were not born to me. Though you and he had different mothers, you share the same father, so you ought to look after each other somewhat, if only to keep others from laughing at you. It seems to me that nothing in this world can be judged with certainty. You were born to one of the Elder Master’s concubines, while that girl Tanchun here was born to one of the Second Master’s; your origins are the same. Now that your mother is dead, one can look back and say that, of your two mothers, yours was ten times the woman that Concubine Zhao is today. You ought therefore to be far superior to that girl Tanchun. How is it that you are not even half her equal? Yet who would have thought it would prove otherwise? Is that not extraordinary? Better to be like me: childless all my life, free of entanglements all my life, and thus safe from other people’s ridicule and gossip.” The married servants attending nearby seized the opportunity to say, “Our young lady is honest and kindhearted. How could she be like Third Miss, with her sharp tongue and clever speech, always determined to get the better of her sisters?

p.src: They know perfectly well what you are like, yet she has not shown you the least consideration.” Lady Xing said, “Even her own brother and sister-in-law treat her so; what can one expect of anyone else?” Before she had finished, a servant announced, “Second Mistress Lian is here.” Lady Xing gave two cold laughs and ordered someone to go out and say, “Tell her to go and nurse her illness. I have no need of her attendance here.” Then one of Tanchun’s young maids came to report, “The Old Lady is awake.” Only then did Lady Xing rise and return to the front apartments. Yingchun escorted her beyond the courtyard and then returned. Xiujú then said, “You see? I told you the other day that the pearl-studded filigree gold phoenix had vanished without anyone knowing where it had gone. Though I reported it to you, you never asked a single question. I said the old nurse must have pawned it to raise money for lending at interest, but you would not believe me and insisted that Siqi had put it away. I asked Siqi; ill though she is, her mind is perfectly clear. When I went to ask her, she said she had not put it away: it had been left for the time being in the box on the bookshelf, since you might need to wear it on the fifteenth of the eighth month. You ought to question the old nurse, but you are too tender-hearted and afraid of giving offense. Now I fear there is no hope of getting it back. When everyone wears hers tomorrow and ours is the only household without one, what will that look like?” Yingchun said, “Why ask? Naturally she only took it away as a temporary loan. I thought she had quietly taken it out and would quietly return it after a little while, and that would be the end of it. Who knew she would forget? And today this trouble has broken out besides. Even if we ask her, I doubt it will do any good.” “Forgotten indeed!” said Xiujú. She has taken your disposition’s measure, and that is why she dares behave like this. I have an idea. I shall go straight to Second Mistress’s rooms and report the matter. She can either send someone to demand it back, or save herself the trouble and give us a few strings of cash to compensate for it. What do you say?” Yingchun hurriedly said, “No, no, no! Let us spare ourselves the trouble. I would rather go without it. Why stir up trouble?” Xiujú said, “Why are you so weak, miss? If everything is to be hushed up for the sake of avoiding trouble, one day they will cheat you out of your very person. I am going.” With that, she started to leave. Yingchun said nothing and could only let her have her way.

p.src: As it happened, the wife of Wang Zhu’er, Yingchun’s wet nurse’s son, had come to ask Yingchun to intercede for her mother-in-law, who had been punished. Hearing them discussing the gold phoenix, she remained outside for the moment. Because Yingchun had always been timid, none of them took her seriously. Now, seeing Xiujú determined to report the matter to Xifeng, she judged that it could no longer be covered up. Since she also had a favor to ask of Yingchun, she had no choice but to enter. Smiling ingratiatingly, she first said to Xiujú, “Miss, do not go making trouble. As for our young mistress’s gold filigree phoenix, our old mistress grew muddle-headed, lost some money gambling, and had no capital with which to win it back, so she borrowed the ornament for a while. She meant to redeem it within a day or half a day, but she never managed to win back her stake, so it has been delayed. By ill luck, someone let the secret slip today and caused this uproar. Even so, it belongs to our mistress, and we would not dare delay indefinitely; we shall certainly redeem it in the end. Now I must also beg our young mistress, for the sake of the bond formed when she nursed at her breast as a child, to go to the Old Lady and plead for mercy, so that the old woman may be released.” Yingchun at once replied, “My good sister-in-law, you had better abandon that foolish hope at once. If you wait for me to intercede, it will do no good even if you wait until next year. Just now even Cousin Baochai, Cousin Daiyu, and all the others pleaded for her, but Grandmother would not consent. What chance would I have alone? I am already overwhelmed with shame myself; am I to go and invite further humiliation?” Xiujú said, “Redeeming the gold phoenix is one matter, and interceding for her is another. Do not muddle the two together. Surely you do not mean that if our mistress will not intercede, you will not redeem it? Sister-in-law, bring back the gold phoenix first; then we can talk.” When Wang Zhu’er’s wife heard Yingchun reject her so firmly and found herself unable to answer Xiujú’s sharp words, she felt humiliated. Knowing full well that Yingchun was habitually mild-tempered, she turned on Xiujú: “Miss, do not presume too much on your position. Look through the whole household: whose mother or nurse does not gain a little advantage by relying on her young master or mistress? Why must everything be accounted for to the last penny only in our case, while you people are free to coax and wheedle things away in secret? Ever since Miss Xing arrived, Her Ladyship ordered that one tael be saved from the monthly allowance and sent to the young lady’s mother. So although Miss Xing’s expenses were added here, the allowance was actually reduced by one tael. Whenever this or that ran short, was it not we who supplied it? Who ever came to demand repayment? We all merely made do as best we could. By now it must amount to at least thirty taels. Has not all the money we have advanced lately simply gone to fill that shortfall?” Before she had finished, Xiujú spat contemptuously and said, “What do you mean, you have paid thirty taels for nothing? Let me settle the account with you: what things has our mistress ever asked you for?”

p.src: When Yingchun heard the woman disclose Lady Xing’s private arrangement, she hastily stopped her: “Enough, enough, enough. If you cannot bring back the gold phoenix, there is no need to drag in all sorts of unrelated matters and shout about them. I do not want the phoenix anymore. Even if the ladies ask about it, I shall merely say it was lost; that will cause you no trouble. You had better go out and rest.” At the same time, she told Xiujú to pour some tea. Both angry and distressed, Xiujú said, “You may not be afraid, miss, but what are we servants here for, if we allow your belongings to be lost? Now she has the insolence to claim that you spent their money, and means to set one sum against the other. If Her Ladyship should ask why you spent all that money, will she not suspect that we servants took advantage in the middle? How could that possibly be allowed?” As she spoke, she began to weep. Siqi could bear it no longer and, ill though she was, forced herself to come over and join Xiujú in questioning the woman. Unable to stop them, Yingchun took up a copy of the Treatise of the Most High on Action and Retribution and began to read.

p.src: The three were still arguing heatedly when Ba آchai, Daiyu, Baoqin, Tanchun, and the others happened to arrive; fearing that Yingchun might be distressed today, they had arranged to come and comfort her. As they entered the courtyard, they heard several people quarrelling. Looking through the gauze window, Tanchun saw Yingchun reclining on the bed with a book, as though she heard nothing. Tanchun could not help smiling. The young maids hurriedly raised the curtain and announced, “The young ladies are here.” Only then did Yingchun put down her book and rise. Seeing that visitors had arrived, and that Tanchun was among them, the woman stopped without needing to be persuaded and seized the chance to leave. After sitting down, Tanchun asked, “Who was speaking here just now? It sounded rather like a quarrel.” Yingchun smiled. “It was nothing. They were merely making a mountain out of a molehill. Why bother asking?” Tanchun smiled. “I distinctly heard something about a ‘gold phoenix,’ and something about ‘having no money and asking us servants for it.’ Who has been asking servants for money? Surely you haven't been asking servants for money, Second Sister? Don't you receive the same monthly allowance and household expenses as the rest of us?” Siqi and Xiuju said, “Exactly so, miss. All the young ladies are treated alike. Each one's money is managed by her nurses and matrons, and even we do not know how the accounts are kept; whenever anything is needed, the young lady merely has to ask. Yet now she insists that our young lady has overspent and that she herself has had to make up a great deal of the difference. But when has our young lady ever asked her for anything?” Tanchun smiled. “Since Second Sister asked her for nothing, perhaps one of us must have asked them instead! Call her back in. I should like to question her myself.” Yingchun smiled. “Now that is absurd. You have nothing to do with the matter. Why should you be dragged into it?” Tanchun smiled. “I do not agree. You and I are alike; your affairs are as much mine as yours. When she speaks against you, she speaks against me too. By the same reasoning, if someone in my household resented me and you heard it, it would be the same as that person resenting you. As mistresses, we naturally do not concern ourselves with trifling money matters; it is true that we simply ask for whatever occurs to us. Now that your mother-in-law has already been found at fault, take this opportunity to appeal to Second Mistress Lian and use some of the money that has not yet been distributed to redeem the ornament. Then the matter will be settled.

p.src: While they were still talking, Pinger suddenly came in. Clapping her hands, Baoqin laughed. “Third Sister, do you possess a magic talisman for summoning spirits and generals?” Daiyu laughed. “This is no mystical Taoist art, but the finest strategy of war: what they call ‘still as a maiden when defending, swift as a cunning hare when striking’—the ingenious tactic of catching the enemy unprepared.” The two continued their teasing. Baochai signalled to them to stop, then changed the subject. When Tanchun saw Pinger, she asked, “Is your mistress feeling any better? Her illness truly seems to have muddled her senses. She pays attention to nothing and lets us suffer such indignities.” Pinger hurriedly asked, “What indignity have you suffered, miss? Who has dared offend you? Please tell me at once.” Zhu'er's wife now panicked. Hurrying up to Pinger, she called, “Miss Pinger, please sit down and let me explain what happened.” Pinger said sternly, “While the young ladies are speaking here, what right have you or I to interrupt? If you had the least sense of propriety, you would be waiting outside. In a place you may not enter without being summoned, when has there ever been a rule allowing married servants from the outer quarters to wander unbidden into the young ladies' rooms?” Xiuju said, “You do not understand. There are no rules in this household; anyone who pleases may come in.” Pinger said, “Then you are all to blame. u.src: While they were still talking, Pinger suddenly came in.
Clapping her hands, Baoqin laughed. “Third Sister, do you possess a magic talisman for summoning spirits and generals?”

Daiyu laughed. “This is no mystical Taoist art, but the finest strategy of war: what they call ‘still as a maiden when defending, swift as a cunning hare when striking’—the ingenious tactic of catching the enemy unprepared.”
The two continued their teasing.
Baochai signalled to them to stop, then changed the subject.
When Tanchun saw Pinger, she asked, “Is your mistress feeling any better?
Her illness truly seems to have muddled her senses. She pays attention to nothing and lets us suffer such indignities.”
Pinger hurriedly asked, “What indignity have you suffered, miss?
Who has dared offend you? Please tell me at once.”
Zhu'er's wife now panicked. Hurrying up to Pinger, she called, “Miss Pinger, please sit down and let me explain what happened.”
Pinger said sternly, “While the young ladies are speaking here, what right have you or I to interrupt?
If you had the least sense of propriety, you would be waiting outside.

p.src: At that moment, Yingchun was absorbed with Baochai in reading stories from the Treatise on Retribution, and had not heard a word of what Tanchun had said. When she suddenly heard Ping'er speak to her in this way, she smiled and said, “There is no use asking me; I have no remedy either. They have done wrong and must bear the consequences themselves. I cannot plead for them, but I shall simply refrain from treating them harshly. As for the things they took without permission, if they return them, I shall accept them; if they do not, I shall let the matter drop. If the ladies question me, I may be able to conceal the matter and smooth it over, and that will be their good fortune. But if I cannot hide it, there is nothing I can do. I cannot deceive the ladies and falsely shield the servants; I shall have no choice but to tell the truth. If you say that I am too easy-tempered and incapable of making a decision, and if you truly have some fine plan that will satisfy everyone without angering the ladies, then deal with them however you please. I shall know nothing about it.” Everyone burst out laughing when they heard this. Daiyu laughed and said, “This truly is ‘speaking of cause and effect while tigers and wolves gather on the palace steps.’ If Second Cousin were a man, how would she ever govern all the many people in this household?” “Exactly,” Yingchun replied with a smile. So many men are just the same; what more can be expected of me?” Before she had finished speaking, another person entered. Who it was remains unknown; listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
